section.title: Thanksgiving and Prayer
section.sectionRationale: Paul opens to a church he has never met, planted by Epaphras, and does two things before he argues anything: he gives thanks for their faith, love, and hope, and he prays that they would be filled with the knowledge of God's will. The greeting and thanksgiving already sound the letter's themes, the gospel bearing fruit worldwide, growth in knowledge, and rescue into the kingdom of God's beloved Son, so that the coming defense of Christ's supremacy rests on a foundation of gratitude and prayer.
section.thesis: Because the gospel has taken root in Colossae and is bearing fruit across the world, Paul thanks God for their faith, love, and hope, and prays they would be filled with the knowledge of God's will, walking worthy of the Lord who has rescued them from darkness into the kingdom of His beloved Son.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the greeting from Paul and Timothy; thanksgiving for the Colossians' faith, love, and hope through the fruitful gospel; and the prayer that they be filled with knowledge and strengthened, giving thanks to the Father who rescued and redeemed them.

units.label: Greeting
units.note: grace and peace to the saints at Colossae

verses.text: Paul, an {{apostolos|apostle}} of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother,
To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace and peace to you from God our Father.

units.label: Thanksgiving for faith, love, and hope

verses.text: We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you,
because we have heard about your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints,
the faith and love proceeding from the hope stored up for you in heaven, of which you have already heard in the word of truth, the {{euangelion|gospel}}
that has come to you. All over the world this gospel is bearing fruit and growing, just as it has been doing among you since the day you heard it and truly understood the grace of God.
You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf,
and who also informed us of your love in the Spirit.

units.label: The prayer and the rescue
units.note: filled with knowledge, brought into the kingdom of the Son

verses.text: For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you and asking God to fill you with the {{epignosis|knowledge}} of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God,
being strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience, and joyfully
giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light.
He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son,
in whom we have {{apolutrosis|redemption}}, the forgiveness of sins.

apostolos.gloss: A sent one, an authorized envoy commissioned to represent the sender. Paul is an apostle of Christ Jesus not by his own ambition but by the will of God, which gives his words to this unvisited church their weight. The title grounds the whole letter: what follows is not private opinion but the message of the risen Christ through His appointed messenger.

euangelion.gloss: Good news, the announcement of a victory or royal accession. Paul calls it the word of truth, a living message that is bearing fruit and growing across the whole world, not a private philosophy. This gospel, and not the speculations threatening Colossae, is what actually produces faith, love, and hope.

epignosis.gloss: Full or thorough knowledge, deeper than mere information; personal, relational understanding. Against a heresy that promised hidden higher knowledge, Paul prays for a knowledge of God's will that is real and complete in Christ. This true knowledge is not abstract but leads to a worthy walk and fruitful obedience.

apolutrosis.gloss: Redemption, release secured by the payment of a ransom, echoing the freeing of slaves and the exodus. In the beloved Son we have redemption, defined here as the forgiveness of sins. The rescue from the dominion of darkness is not vague; it is purchased release into the kingdom of Christ.

basic.context: Paul writes to a church he has never visited, in the town of Colossae, founded through his coworker Epaphras. Before he confronts the false teaching that is unsettling them, he gives thanks for their faith, love, and hope, and tells them how he prays for them. He wants them filled with the true knowledge of God, so they can live lives that please the Lord who has already rescued them from darkness.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real letter to a real congregation, and its opening thanksgiving and prayer set up everything that follows. Paul is not just being polite; he is naming the gospel that saved them and the growth he longs to see, so that when he defends the greatness of Christ, they already know they belong to Him. The prayer shows us what to ask God for in one another.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul writes as an apostolos, a sent one commissioned by God. He is thankful for their grip on the euangelion, the good news that is bearing fruit worldwide. He prays they would be filled with epignosis, real and full knowledge of God's will, over against a heresy promising secret knowledge. And he rejoices that in the Son they have apolutrosis, redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
basic.typology: Being rescued from the dominion of darkness and brought into a kingdom echoes the exodus, when God redeemed Israel out of slavery into His own care. Sharing in the inheritance of the saints in the light recalls Israel receiving its inheritance in the land. Christ is the greater deliverer, and His people the true inheritors.
basic.christ: Everything here flows to and through Christ. Faith is in Christ Jesus, hope is stored up in heaven, and rescue means being brought into the kingdom of God's beloved Son. In Him, and in no one else, we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins. Even before the great hymn of chapter one, Christ is already the center.
basic.god: God is the Father who is thanked, prayed to, and praised. He fills His people with knowledge, strengthens them with His glorious might, qualifies them for the inheritance, rescues them from darkness, and gives them His beloved Son. Salvation is His initiative from start to finish.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 1 opens with a similar thanksgiving and prayer for knowledge and strength. Philippians 1 shows Paul thanking God and praying for a church's growth in love and discernment. And Acts 26 records Christ sending Paul to turn people from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God.
basic.oneStory: This opening plants the letter in the big story: a people once in darkness are redeemed and brought into the kingdom of God's Son, just as Israel was brought out of Egypt into the inheritance. The gospel that began in Colossae is spreading through the whole world, carrying the hope of glory to the nations.

context.literary:
Verses 3 to 8 are one long sentence in Greek, and verses 9 to 14 are another. The English of the BSB breaks them up, but the original rolls forward on a chain of relative clauses and participles, each one handing the reader to the next: the faith and love, the hope that feeds them, the gospel that brought the hope, the Epaphras who brought the gospel. The effect is of a single gratitude unrolling through the whole church's history, from heaven's storehouse to a Colossian living room.

The two halves have a mirrored shape. The thanksgiving is about what God has already done, 'we have heard,' 'you heard,' 'you learned.' The prayer is about what Paul asks for next, 'filled,' 'walk,' 'strengthened.' Each half is held together by the same small pair of verbs. The gospel is 'bearing fruit and growing' in verse 6, and the Colossians are asked to be 'bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God' in verse 10. What the gospel does everywhere, Paul prays it will do in them.

The word 'all' keeps returning: all the saints, all over the world, all spiritual wisdom, in every way, every good work, all power. Paul is quietly building a vocabulary of fullness against teachers who offered a select few a secret higher tier. He also sets out the triad of faith, love and hope in verses 4 and 5, but in an unusual order. Hope is not a third item added at the end but the source from which the first two proceed.

The passage ends by pointing to 'His beloved Son' in verse 13 and the redemption 'in whom' we have in verse 14. That turn from the Father who rescues to the Son who redeems is the hinge into the hymn of verses 15 to 20, which begins with a relative clause that picks up directly from 'in whom.' The opening prayer is therefore not an introduction that can be skipped. It is the ramp onto the great statement about Christ.
context.historical:
Colossae lay in the Lycus Valley in what is now western Turkey, a few miles from the larger and richer cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis. It had been a more significant town in earlier centuries, but by Paul's day it was overshadowed by its neighbours. Paul had not been there, Colossians 2:1. The church had been planted through Epaphras, a local man, verse 7, whom Paul later describes as one of them, wrestling in prayer for them and for the believers at Laodicea and Hierapolis, Colossians 4:12-13.

Paul writes from prison, with Timothy named alongside him, as in several of his letters. The letter travels with Tychicus and with Onesimus, Colossians 4:7-9, the runaway slave of Philemon who belonged to the same town. The same carrier and the same circle make Colossians and Philemon close companions, and the greeting 'grace and peace' ties both to the wider Pauline mission.

The pressure on the church seems to have come from teaching that mixed Jewish observances with a preoccupation with angels and ascetic discipline, Colossians 2:16-23. That background explains the emphasis on 'knowledge' and 'wisdom' and 'understanding' in verse 9, words that the rivals claimed as their own. Paul reclaims them. Knowledge is not a secret tier but the knowledge of God's will, and it is given to the whole church, not to an elite.

The imagery of verses 12 to 14 would have been vivid to any Jewish or God-fearing listener. 'Inheritance' recalled the allotment of the land to the tribes. 'Redemption' recalled the exodus. 'Darkness' and 'dominion' recalled Egypt and every empire since. Gentile believers who had never known the story of Israel are being told that it is now theirs, and that they have been brought into a kingdom with a king who loves them.
context.canonical:
Paul's thanksgiving belongs to a whole habit of prayer that runs through his letters, but it also draws on older strands. The triad of faith, love and hope appears in 1 Thessalonians 1:3, in Romans 5:1-5, and in the famous climax of 1 Corinthians 13:13. Here, as there, hope is not wishful thinking but a reality secured by God, which Peter calls an inheritance 'kept in heaven for you,' 1 Peter 1:3-4. Verse 5 therefore belongs to a broad New Testament conviction that the future is already stored up.

The prayer for knowledge echoes the promise of Isaiah 11:9 that the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD, and Jeremiah 31:34, where all would know Him. The New Testament takes up the same hope in Philippians 1:9-11 and Ephesians 1:17-19 and 3:16-19, where Paul asks for the same cluster of knowledge, strength and fruit. The call to walk worthy runs through Ephesians 4:1 and 1 Thessalonians 2:12.

The language of rescue and inheritance gathers up the whole exodus story. The LORD told Moses He would redeem Israel from slavery, Exodus 6:6, and Deuteronomy 7:8 looks back on it as the day He redeemed them from the house of slavery. Israel's inheritance was the land. Paul reframes both: the rescue is from the dominion of darkness, and the inheritance is shared 'in the light.' Acts 26:18 records the commission given to Paul himself, to turn people from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among the sanctified. The same pairs, darkness and light, forgiveness and inheritance, appear in his own letter.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant this opening to do three things for a church he had never met. First, it was meant to establish common ground. He does not begin with the problem. He begins with what he has heard about them and what he thanks God for, so that when he later warns them he is speaking as a friend who already believes the best. The thanksgiving is sincere, and it is also tactful.

Second, he meant to correct the shape of their ambitions. The false teaching on offer promised depth and fullness through special knowledge and ritual. Paul prays for the same things, knowledge, wisdom, strength, but describes them as the possession of every ordinary believer and shows that they are measured by a changed life: fruit, endurance, patience, joy and thanks. Real depth is a way of walking, not a body of secrets.

Third, he meant to anchor them in a finished rescue. Verses 12 to 14 do not ask God to deliver them but tell them He has already done so. 'Has qualified,' 'has rescued,' 'brought,' are past events. The readers are being asked to live from a settled position, not toward one. Everything that follows in the letter is an argument that they need nothing added to what they already have in the Son.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage mixes report, prayer and statement of fact. The report of verses 3 to 8 describes what had happened in Colossae and is not an instruction. The prayer of verses 9 to 12 is not a command to the church but a request to God, though it tells believers what to ask for one another. The statements of verses 12 to 14 describe what God has done and are the foundation for the commands that come later.

What carries over to the present is the pattern. Churches are meant to give thanks for what God is doing in other churches and to pray for them by name, as Paul prays for Colossae without having visited. The content of the prayer is a model: knowledge of God's will, a life that pleases Him, fruit, endurance, joy and thanks. It also corrects a common instinct. Many pray for relief first. Paul prays for strength 'so that you may have full endurance and patience,' which assumes that hardship is coming and that the aim is faithfulness in it. The rescue of verses 13 and 14 is not a promise of ease but a statement of where believers now belong.

debates.question: Is 'hope' in verse 5 the thing hoped for or the act of hoping?

views.label: The object, a secured inheritance
views.case: Paul says the hope is 'stored up for you in heaven,' which makes it a thing kept safe, not a feeling in the heart. The same idea appears in 1 Peter 1:4, an inheritance kept in heaven. On this reading faith and love grow because the believer knows something real is waiting.

views.label: The attitude, confident expectation
views.case: Some read hope as the subjective trust that looks forward, since Paul says faith and love 'proceed from' it, and a mood or disposition seems the likelier source of action. Verse 23 also speaks of not being moved from the hope of the gospel, a phrase that can mean the standing attitude of the believer.

views.label: Both together
views.case: The Greek word elpis commonly carries both senses, and Paul can move between them. The hope in heaven is the ground, and the hoping is the believer's response, as in Romans 8:24-25.

debates.bearing: Either way, hope is anchored outside the believer. Paul's point is that love and faith do not feed on themselves but on a promise held for them by God.

debates.question: Is the kingdom of the Son in verse 13 already here or still to come?

views.label: Already, in a real but hidden form
views.case: The verbs are in the past: God 'has rescued' and 'brought us into' the kingdom. Believers are already citizens, as Philippians 3:20 and Ephesians 2:6 also say. The kingdom is present wherever the Son's rule is acknowledged.

views.label: Future, with a present foretaste
views.case: Elsewhere the kingdom is something to be inherited, 1 Corinthians 15:24 and Matthew 25:34, and Paul speaks in this very passage of an 'inheritance' stored up in heaven. On this reading the language of verse 13 is the language of a decisive transfer whose fullness has yet to arrive.

debates.bearing: Scripture holds both. The change of allegiance is complete and the manifestation is still coming. The practical consequence in Colossians is that believers are to live as those who already belong to the new kingdom while they wait for its open reign.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's prayer is dense with words that repay slow reading. The most important is epignosis, 'knowledge,' in verses 9 and 10. It is a compound of the ordinary word for knowledge, gnosis, with a prefix that suggests full or accurate recognition. Paul prays that the Colossians would be filled with the epignosis of God's will, and then that they would grow in the epignosis of God. The knowledge in view is not information about God but a deepening acquaintance with Him, and it is tied to the will of God and to a changed way of life. Against teachers who offered special gnosis to initiates, Paul's request is for something offered to every believer.

The verb of verse 9, plerothete, 'fill,' is in the passive voice, a request for something God does. The same stem lies behind the fullness that the letter later says dwells in Christ, verse 19. The prayer is that a church receive from the Son something of the fullness that is in Him.

The call to 'walk' in verse 10, peripateo, is the Hebrew idiom of conduct translated into Greek, a way of living measured step by step. Paul asks them to walk 'worthily,' axios, of the Lord, a word that suggests a balanced weight: a life that matches its source. It is followed by the clause 'to please Him in every way,' areskeia, which is rare, and by a pair of participles, 'bearing fruit' and 'growing.' The same two participles, karpophoroumenon kai auxanomenon, were used of the gospel in verse 6. The gospel's path in the world and the believer's path in the Christian life are described in the same words.

Verse 11 piles up the vocabulary of power. 'Strengthened' is a present passive participle, dynamoumenoi, 'being empowered,' a continuing action. 'Power' is dynamis and 'might' is kratos, the second often used of the sovereign strength of God, as in Ephesians 1:19. The surprising thing is what the power is for. It is not for wonders but for hypomone, 'endurance,' the ability to stay under a burden, and makrothymia, 'patience,' literally long-temperedness. The power of God is shown in the Colossians' capacity to bear and wait.

In verse 12 the verb hikanoo, 'qualified,' means to make sufficient, to give someone the standing needed. Paul uses the same root in 2 Corinthians 3:6, where God has made the apostles competent as ministers of a new covenant. The Colossians did not make themselves fit for the inheritance; the Father made them so. 'Inheritance,' kleros, is the old word for an allotted portion, used in the Septuagint of the land divided among Israel's tribes, and it is here claimed for a church of Gentiles.

Verse 13 uses two pictures. 'Rescued,' rhyomai, is the word of a deliverer snatching someone out of danger. 'Dominion,' exousia, is the word for authority, and the 'dominion of darkness' is a regime with real claims. 'Brought,' methistemi, means to move someone from one place to another, to transfer. Verse 14 closes with apolutrosis, 'redemption,' a buying out, defined by the word that follows it, aphesis, 'forgiveness,' a sending away. One word names the price paid and the other names the result. The BSB footnote notes that a late tradition adds 'through His blood,' which is not in the earliest manuscripts but is plainly the sense of Colossians 1:20.

typology.type: Rescue from the dominion of darkness, Colossians 1:13 and the exodus
typology.fulfillment: The LORD told Moses He would bring Israel out from under the burdens of Egypt and redeem them with an outstretched arm, Exodus 6:6, and Deuteronomy 7:8 remembers it as redemption from the house of slavery. The correspondence in Paul's language is exact: rescue, redemption and a people moved into the care of a new Lord. The escalation is that the tyrant is not Pharaoh but the dominion of darkness, and the rescue price is not a lamb's blood but the Son's, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The type falls short in that Israel was freed from a place, while believers are freed from sin and its authority, Acts 26:18, and brought into a kingdom with no border to cross again.

typology.type: The inheritance of the saints in the light, Colossians 1:12
typology.fulfillment: Israel's inheritance was an allotment of land, divided among the tribes by lot, Joshua 14:1-2. Paul uses the same word for a share that Gentile believers hold. The correspondence is of a gift received and not earned, kept for a people by God. The escalation is that the land was a pointer to something greater, Hebrews 4:8-9 and 11:13-16, and that the inheritance is now described as 'in the light' and 'stored up in heaven,' verse 5. It is also shared with Christ, Romans 8:17. The type falls short because land could be lost and was lost in exile, while this inheritance cannot perish or fade, 1 Peter 1:4.

typology.type: A people qualified by the Father, the priests of the old covenant
typology.fulfillment: No Israelite became fit to draw near to God by his own effort. Aaron's sons were washed, clothed and anointed before they could serve, Exodus 29:4-9. The word Paul uses in verse 12, 'qualified,' belongs to this world of a status conferred. The correspondence is that fitness is given from outside. The escalation is that the Colossians, Gentiles and ordinary believers, are made fit to share the lot of the saints in the light, not merely to serve at a sanctuary, Revelation 1:6 and 1 Peter 2:9. The type is partial, since the old priests were a class set apart and the people of the new covenant are all qualified.

study.christ:
This passage sets the Son on the stage in two quiet phrases before the hymn begins, and both repay attention. The first is 'the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ' in verse 3. Paul addresses the God he thanks by naming His relationship to Jesus. The God of Israel is not first the God of heaven in the abstract but the Father of a Person, and the Colossians come to Him through that Person. Paul does the same in Romans 15:6 and 2 Corinthians 1:3, so the habit is deliberate.

The second is 'His beloved Son' in verse 13, literally 'the Son of His love.' The phrase echoes the voice at Jesus' baptism, 'This is My beloved Son,' Matthew 3:17, and the cry of the Father in the parable of the vineyard, Mark 12:6. The kingdom believers belong to is described as the Son's, and the Son is loved. It is not an impersonal realm but a household governed by a King whom the Father adores. To be brought into it is to be brought into the Father's love for His Son.

The work of Christ is stated in verse 14 as redemption and forgiveness 'in whom.' The location matters. Redemption is not something Christ hands out from a distance; it is found in Him, so that being in Christ is the whole of the blessing. Paul goes on in Ephesians 1:7 to say that in Him we have redemption through His blood. The cost is stated more fully in Colossians 1:20, 'by making peace through the blood of His cross,' and in 1 Peter 1:18-19, which speaks of redemption by the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish. The exodus pattern is thus fulfilled: Israel was redeemed by the blood of a lamb on the doorposts, Exodus 12:13, and believers are redeemed by the Lamb of God.

Christ is also the hope. Verse 5 speaks of a hope stored up in heaven, and verse 27, later in the letter, says the mystery is 'Christ in you, the hope of glory.' The thing stored for the believer is not distinct from the Person who holds it. Paul says in Colossians 3:3-4 that the believer's life is hidden with Christ in God and that when Christ appears, they will appear with Him in glory.

Christ is the content of the gospel that bears fruit. The 'word of truth' of verse 5 and the 'grace of God' of verse 6 are two names for the same message, and Acts 20:24 calls it the gospel of the grace of God. It is a person's rescue, not a philosophy. In the context of the Colossian error this is a decisive point: no extra teaching or rule is needed alongside the Son. A caution is in order. The passage does not itself unfold who Christ is; it points forward to the hymn, where the claims are spelled out. What it provides is the setting: gratitude to the Father for a rescue found entirely in the Son.
study.god:
God appears in this opening mostly as the Father, and the title carries more weight than it seems. He is 'God our Father' in verse 2, the Father of the Lord Jesus in verse 3, and 'the Father' of verse 12 who has qualified the saints. In each place Paul grounds the relationship in what the Father has done. He is not a remote deity to be placated but the One who adopts, fits and brings His people home. For the doctrine of God, the passage shows that fatherhood is first a fact about His relationship to the Son and then, by grace, about His relationship to believers.

He is the God who acts first. Everything in the passage is traced to His initiative: the gospel that has come, the grace that was understood, the filling with knowledge, the strength, the qualification, the rescue, the transfer. The Colossians' faith and love are real, but they proceed from a hope that God stores up. The human verbs, 'heard,' 'learned,' 'walk,' are responses to a God who has already moved. This keeps the passage from being read as a ladder of achievement.

He is the God who gives knowledge of His will. The prayer assumes that God wants to be known and that His will is not hidden in a secret that only a few can reach. The knowledge He gives is practical: it shapes a walk, bears fruit, and grows. A God who reveals Himself so that His people can please Him is a God of generosity and not of withholding. This answers the false teaching, which treated God's will as something a select few could unlock.

He is powerful and gives power for endurance. Verse 11 speaks of 'His glorious might,' and the surprising use of that might is patience and joy. God's strength is shown in how His people stand firm and give thanks, not in a display. It fits the God of the exodus who delivered Israel and then carried them through the wilderness.

He is a God who rescues from a rival dominion. The 'dominion of darkness' is not an equal power but a regime from which the Father transfers people by a decisive act. His sovereignty is not in doubt, and His mercy takes the form of redemption and forgiveness. The result is a kingdom owned by the Son He loves.

For worship, the passage models gratitude as the first response. Paul gives thanks 'always,' and he asks that the Colossians would live 'joyfully giving thanks to the Father.' Thankfulness is not a mood but a recognition of who has done what, and it grows as believers learn to see the whole of their lives, from rescue to inheritance, as a gift.

crossReferences.note: Paul's thanksgiving and prayer for the Ephesians follows the same pattern as Colossians 1: news of their faith and love, thanks, and a request for wisdom, knowledge and strength. It shows that Colossians 1:9-14 is not a one-off but a template of apostolic prayer, and it carries the prayer on into the power that raised Christ.

Paul prays that love would abound in knowledge and depth of insight so that the readers may be pure and blameless, filled with the fruit of righteousness. The vocabulary of knowledge, fruit and a life that pleases God matches Colossians 1:9-10 closely, and shows how Paul links doctrine and conduct in his prayers.

Paul remembers the Thessalonians' work of faith, labour of love and endurance of hope. This is the earliest appearance of the triad of faith, love and hope in Paul, and it shows that Colossians 1:4-5 draws on a settled pattern of describing a healthy church.

Peter speaks of a living hope and an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade, kept in heaven for believers. It confirms that the hope 'stored up' in Colossians 1:5 is a secured reality, and it ties the inheritance to the resurrection of Jesus.

In Paul's own account of his commission, he is sent to open eyes so that people turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, receiving forgiveness of sins and a place among the sanctified. Colossians 1:12-14 is a close echo, showing that Paul's letter language is shaped by his own call.

God promises to bring Israel out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, to free them from slavery, and to redeem them with an outstretched arm. This is the background to the redemption and rescue of Colossians 1:13-14, and it shows why a Gentile church could be told it had been through an exodus.

Paul says Epaphras, who is one of the Colossians, is always wrestling in prayer for them that they may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. It gives a face to the prayer of 1:9-12 and shows that the one who planted the church also prays in the same terms Paul does.

Paul traces a line from faith to peace, from hope in the glory of God to endurance that produces character. It sheds light on why hope, in Colossians 1:5, is the source of love and faith, and why endurance and patience in 1:11 are seen as the fruit of God's power.

Moses explains that the LORD brought Israel out with a mighty hand and redeemed them from the house of slavery because He loved them. The reason given is love, and it prepares the way for 'the Son of His love' in Colossians 1:13, a kingdom founded on affection.

The prophet says that the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. Paul's prayer that the Colossians be filled with the knowledge of God, and his report that the gospel is bearing fruit all over the world, are early fulfillments of that expectation.

Paul speaks of the blessed hope, the appearing of our great God and Savior Christ Jesus, who gave Himself to redeem us from all wickedness. It joins hope, redemption and a purified people in a way that matches Colossians 1:5 and 1:13-14.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with humanity placed in a garden to be fruitful, to know God and to walk with Him in the cool of the day. Genesis 3 describes how that knowledge was lost and the walk broken, and Genesis 3:24 shows the pair driven east. Everything in Colossians 1:1-14 is a movement back. The gospel bears fruit and grows, as humanity was told to do in Genesis 1:28. The Colossians are asked to know God and to walk in a manner worthy of Him. The exile is reversed in the rescue of verse 13.

The passage also gathers up the exodus and the land. The great rescue story of the Old Testament was Israel's deliverance from Egypt, remembered in every Passover and every psalm, and the great hope was the land given as an inheritance. Paul tells Gentile believers that both belong to them. They have been redeemed, they have been moved into a kingdom, and they share in an inheritance. Israel's story is not discarded but widened, as God promised to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3.

There is a forward movement as well. The 'hope stored up in heaven' is the entry to the future the prophets saw. Isaiah foretold a world full of the knowledge of the LORD, Isaiah 11:9, and Daniel saw the kingdom given to the saints of the Most High, Daniel 7:18. Paul declares that the kingdom has begun, in the Son, while its public reign is yet to come. The believers in Colossae are therefore at once heirs and exiles: they belong to a kingdom whose King is hidden, and they walk, endure and give thanks until He appears.

The story ends in the new creation, where the light that is here the believers' inheritance fills everything. Revelation 21:23-24 speaks of a city that has no need of sun or moon, because the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb. Revelation 22:5 says there will be no more night. The dominion of darkness will be gone, the knowledge of God will be full, and the Father's Son will be loved and honoured by a redeemed people from every nation. The prayer of Colossians 1 will have been answered completely.

quiz.q: What three things does Paul give thanks for in the Colossians?

options.text: Their faith in Christ, love for the saints, and hope stored up in heaven.
options.note: Verses 4 and 5 name the classic triad of faith, love, and hope.

options.text: Their wealth, influence, and social standing.
options.note: Paul gives thanks for spiritual fruit, not worldly advantage.

options.text: Their secret knowledge and visionary experiences.
options.note: That is the false teaching Paul opposes, not what he commends.

options.text: Nothing yet, since he had never met them.
options.note: Paul thanks God for them constantly, having heard of their faith.

quiz.q: What does Paul say the gospel is doing all over the world?

options.text: Bearing fruit and growing, just as it has among the Colossians.
options.note: Verse 6 pictures the gospel as a living, spreading, fruitful word.

options.text: Fading away as new philosophies replace it.
options.note: The opposite; Paul stresses its growth, not its decline.

options.text: Remaining hidden to all but a spiritual elite.
options.note: The gospel has come openly to them and to the whole world.

options.text: Producing division and confusion everywhere.
options.note: It bears the fruit of faith, love, and hope, not confusion.

quiz.q: What is the main thing Paul prays for the Colossians?

options.text: That they be filled with the knowledge of God's will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding.
options.note: Verse 9 is the heart of the prayer, leading to a worthy walk.

options.text: That they gain wealth and comfort.
options.note: Paul prays for knowledge, endurance, and fruitfulness, not comfort.

options.text: That they escape all hardship immediately.
options.note: He prays for endurance and patience within hardship, not escape from it.

options.text: That they keep the teaching secret.
options.note: The gospel is proclaimed openly and spreads; nothing is kept secret.

quiz.q: According to verses 13 and 14, what has God done for believers?

options.text: Rescued them from darkness into the kingdom of His Son, in whom they have redemption and forgiveness.
options.note: These verses summarize the great rescue and its ground in Christ.

options.text: Left them to rescue themselves by effort.
options.note: The rescue is God's act; He has rescued and brought them in.

options.text: Given them a set of rules to earn acceptance.
options.note: Redemption is by Christ, not by rule-keeping, as chapter two argues.

options.text: Promised a rescue that has not yet begun.
options.note: The verbs are past: He has rescued and brought them in already.

quiz.q: Why does the true knowledge of God's will matter, according to verse 10?

options.text: So that believers walk worthy of the Lord, please Him, bear fruit, and grow.
options.note: Knowledge here is not abstract; it produces a worthy, fruitful life.

options.text: So that believers can win arguments and feel superior.
options.note: The aim is a pleasing walk, not pride or debate.

options.text: So that believers can unlock hidden spiritual powers.
options.note: That echoes the false teaching, not Paul's purpose.

options.text: It does not matter much; only feelings count.
options.note: Paul prays earnestly for this knowledge as the root of godly living.

questions: Paul gives thanks for the Colossians before he corrects them. Who are the believers you could thank God for by name this week, and what fruit do you see in them?
Paul prays for knowledge that leads to a worthy walk, not just information. Where is God calling you to turn what you know about His will into how you actually live?
The gospel is described as bearing fruit and growing worldwide. Where have you seen it bearing fruit in your own life, and where do you long to see more growth?
God has rescued you from the dominion of darkness into the kingdom of His Son. How would living as a rescued citizen of that kingdom change how you face this week?
Christian hope is stored up safely in heaven, outside our circumstances. When life feels shaky, how does an anchored hope steady your faith and love right now?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts read and the Lord Jesus Christ after God our Father; the BSB follows the shorter reading, which does not change the sense.
Who has qualified you can also be rendered qualified us in some manuscripts; either way the Father is the one who makes His people fit for the inheritance.
